<reason>Side A built the cleaner marginal-contribution case: universities control the fastest-moving demand dial when vacancy is near zero, and a severe-shortage cap freezes growth rather than eliminating existing fees or students. A answered the purpose-built housing challenge with a persuasive overflow mechanism and gave external, liftable criteria for "severe." Side B's root-cause and cross-subsidy points remained live but were weakened by misattributing the segregation claim and by proposing a secured-bed precondition, which A convincingly framed as conceding that recruitment cannot remain unconstrained.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 "both, in sequence" answer: purpose-built beds absorb students only until built capacity is exceeded, after which overflow competes for shared and family housing. Its closing then turned B's bed-guarantee alternative into an admission that some binding recruitment limit is necessary.</best_rebuttal>
